title: Demand for apples
questionText: Consider the demand for apples. Suppose that the price of apples falls to $4 per kg. What will happen to the demand for apples?
answers: There will be a contraction in demand
There will be an expansion in demand
There will be an increase in demand
There will be a decrease in demand
explanation: A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift. A lower price means more is demanded — an expansion.

title: Demand for lemonade
questionText: Consider the demand for lemonade. Suppose that the price of lemonade increased from $2 per can to $3 per can. What would happen to the demand for lemonade?
answers: There will be a decrease in demand from 60 cans to 40 cans
There will be an increase in demand from 40 cans to 60 cans
There will be a contraction in demand from 60 cans to 40 cans
There will be an expansion in demand from 40 cans to 60 cans
explanation: The good’s own price rose, so we move along the curve. A higher price reduces quantity demanded — a contraction — from 60 to 40 cans.

questionText: Which of the following would cause a movement along the demand curve for coffee, rather than a shift of the whole curve?
answers: A fall in the price of coffee
A rise in the incomes of coffee drinkers
A fall in the price of tea, a substitute for coffee
A health report praising the benefits of drinking coffee
explanation: Only a change in the good’s own price moves us along its demand curve. Income, substitute prices and health reports all shift the whole curve.

title: Demand for cars
questionText: Consider the demand curve for cars. Suppose that due to strong economic growth there is an increase in income levels amongst the population. What would happen to the demand for cars?
answers: There would be a decrease in demand for cars
There would be an expansion in the demand for cars
There would be a contraction in the demand for cars
There would be an increase in demand for cars
explanation: Cars are a normal good, so higher incomes shift the whole demand curve to the right — an increase in demand, not a movement along it.

title: Demand for the children's toy
questionText: A viral marketing campaign on social media for a children’s toy makes it the ‘must have’ Christmas present. How will this affect demand for the toy?
answers: There will be an increase in demand for the toy
There will be a decrease in demand for the toy
There will be an expansion in demand for the toy
There will be a contraction in demand for the toy
explanation: A viral ‘must-have’ campaign changes tastes and preferences, shifting the whole demand curve right — an increase in demand.

questionText: Increased immigration leads to an increase in demand for hospitality services. What factor affecting demand best explains this shift?
answers: Price changes
Changes in tastes and preferences
Change in the number of consumers
Changes in the price of substitutes
explanation: More people means more consumers in the market. A change in the number of consumers shifts demand right.

title: Demand for Switch games
questionText: Consider the demand curve for Nintendo Switch games. Suppose the price of Switch games falls from $60 to $40. What happens to the demand for Switch games?
answers: There will be an increase in demand from 80 to 120 games
There will be a contraction in demand from 120 to 80 games
There will be a decrease in demand from 120 to 80 games
There will be an expansion in demand from 80 to 120 games
explanation: A fall in the good’s own price is a movement along the curve. Lower price raises quantity demanded — an expansion — from 80 to 120 games.

questionText: Suppose that the price of Nintendo Switch games reduce. What would be the likely impact on the demand for Nintendo Switch consoles?
answers: No change in demand
An increase in demand
An expansion in demand
A decrease in demand
explanation: Games and consoles are complements. Cheaper games make consoles more attractive, shifting demand for consoles right — an increase.

questionText: Consider the data table below showing price changes for two substitute goods. Given the data, what is likely to happen to the demand for Good A in year 2?
answers: There will be an increase in demand for Good A
There will be a contraction in demand for Good A
There will be no change in demand for Good A
There will be a decrease in demand for Good A
explanation: Good B (a substitute) became cheaper, so consumers switch to it. Demand for Good A shifts left — a decrease.

questionText: Consider the same data table below showing price changes for two substitute goods. Given the data, what is likely to happen to the demand for Good B in year 2?
answers: There will be an increase in demand for Good B
There will be a decrease in demand for Good B
There will be an expansion in demand for Good B
There will be a contraction in demand for Good B
explanation: Good B’s own price fell, so we move along its own demand curve. A lower price raises quantity demanded — an expansion.

title: Demand for Snickers bars
questionText: What statement would most likely be correct if the price of Mars bars was to reduce?
answers: There would be a decrease in demand for Snickers bars at all price levels
There would be a decrease in demand for Snickers bars at $2 only
There would be a decrease in the demand for Snickers bars below $2
There would be a contraction in demand for Snickers bars
explanation: Cheaper Mars bars (a substitute) shift the whole Snickers curve left, so demand falls at every price level — not just at one price.

title: Demand for coffee
questionText: A health report praises the benefits of coffee, shifting demand from D1 to D2. At a price of $5, by how much has the demand for coffee increased?
answers: By 50 cups per day
By 150 cups per day
By 100 cups per day
By 200 cups per day
explanation: Read the horizontal gap between D1 and D2 at $5: quantity demanded rises by 100 cups per day.

title: Demand for beef
questionText: Following a health scare, the demand for beef shifts from D1 to D2. At a price of $6 per kg, by how much has the demand for beef decreased?
answers: By 80 kg
By 40 kg
By 60 kg
By 100 kg
explanation: Read the horizontal gap between D1 and D2 at $6 per kg: quantity demanded falls by 80 kg.

title: Demand for Coca-Cola
questionText: Consider the demand curves shown for Coca-Cola. What could explain the shift from D1 to D2?
answers: There has been an increase in the price of Coca-Cola
There has been a decrease in the price of Coca-Cola
There has been a decrease in the price of Pepsi
There has been an increase in the price of Pepsi
explanation: The rightward shift is an increase in demand. A dearer substitute (Pepsi) makes consumers switch to Coca-Cola; a change in Coke’s own price would only move along the curve.

title: Demand for iPads
questionText: Consider the demand curve for iPads. Suppose Apple announces that the price of iPads will be reduced by 20% in one month’s time. What will happen to the demand for iPads today?
answers: There will be an increase in demand for iPads
There will be a decrease in demand for iPads
There will be an expansion in demand for iPads
There will be a contraction in demand for iPads
explanation: Expecting a price cut next month, consumers delay buying, so demand today shifts left — a decrease. The current price hasn’t changed, so it’s a shift, not a contraction.

title: Demand for iPads
questionText: Consider the same demand curve for iPads. One month has passed and the price of iPads falls by 20%. What happens to the demand for iPads?
answers: There will be an increase in demand for iPads
There will be a decrease in demand for iPads
There will be an expansion in demand for iPads
There will be a contraction in demand for iPads
explanation: Now the good’s own price actually falls, so we move along the curve — an expansion in quantity demanded.

title: Demand for cinema tickets
questionText: A recession causes rising unemployment and a 5% reduction in the average income of workers in an economy. How would this affect the demand for cinema tickets?
answers: There will be a decrease in demand for cinema tickets by 5%
There will be an unknown decrease in demand for cinema tickets
There will be an increase in the demand for cinema tickets by 5%
There will be an unknown increase in demand for cinema tickets
explanation: Lower incomes decrease demand for cinema tickets (a normal good), but a 5% income fall doesn’t translate into a precise 5% fall in demand — the size is unknown.

An increase in the price of a complementary good

An increase in the price of a complementary good
An increase in the price of a substitute
A decrease in the price of a complementary good
A decrease in the price of a substitute
A decrease in the price of a complementary good
questionText: What two factors could cause a decrease in demand?
answers: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D
explanation: Demand falls when a substitute gets cheaper (consumers switch away) and when a complement gets dearer (the pair is bought less) — that is Row A.

title: Demand for streaming subscriptions
questionText: A rise in household incomes shifts the demand for streaming subscriptions from D1 to D2. At a price of $10 per month, what quantity is now demanded, and how should the change be described?
answers: 150 subscriptions, an increase of 120
270 subscriptions, an increase of 120
270 subscriptions, an expansion of 120
150 subscriptions, an expansion of 120
explanation: The rightward shift is an increase in demand. At $10, D2 gives 270 subscriptions, up 120 from 150. It is an ‘increase’ (a shift), not an ‘expansion’.

title: Demand for scooters
questionText: Given the demand curve for scooters, what would cause a contraction in demand of 80 scooters?
answers: A price decrease to $60
A price decrease to $45
A price increase to $90
A price increase to $105
explanation: A contraction is a movement up the demand curve caused by a higher own price. Raising the price to $105 reduces quantity demanded by 80 scooters.
